summary: Describes TreeDN, a tree-based content delivery network architecture for live streaming to very large audiences. It aims to reduce the strain such events put on network resources as bitrates climb.

eli5.summary: Rather than sending a copy of a live show to every viewer from one far place, it passes copies along branches of a tree, so each road carries fewer copies.

questions: multicast approach for live streaming at scale
subtitle: A tree-shaped network delivering one stream to millions of viewers without duplication

tldr.problem: Live streaming to millions of viewers over the Internet wastes bandwidth by sending duplicate copies of the same content to each viewer individually, and IP multicast failed to gain Internet-wide adoption due to complexity and the "all or nothing" problem.
tldr.mechanism: TreeDN combines simplified Source-Specific Multicast (SSM) on native multicast networks with Automatic Multicast Tunneling (AMT) overlays to reach unicast-only networks, enabling efficient tree-based replication that works incrementally.
tldr.outcome: Operators can offer Replication-as-a-Service to content providers at a fraction of the cost of traditional unicast CDNs, with live deployments on GEANT, RARE, and EUMETCast networks already running successfully.

facts.label: Key multicast protocols supported
facts.value: PIM-SSM, mLDP, BIER, Segment Routing, BGP-MVPN

facts.label: Multicast group specification
facts.value: IGMPv3 (IPv4) or MLDv2 (IPv6) with source and group address

facts.label: Operational benefit
facts.value: Marginal cost per additional viewer approaches zero

facts.label: Example use cases
facts.value: Live sports, concerts, 4K/8K video, satellite data distribution, AR events

today: RFC 9706 is an Informational RFC published in January 2025 and has not been obsoleted. TreeDN architectures are currently operational on research networks (GEANT, RARE) and are delivering real services (EUMETCast Terrestrial meteorological data) to production users.

sections.title: The Challenge of Live Streaming to Millions
sections.content: When a major sporting event, concert, or news event is streamed live to the Internet, the sheer number of simultaneous viewers creates unprecedented demand. As bitrates rise to support 4K and 8K video or Augmented Reality, the load on network infrastructure becomes extreme. Traditional Content Delivery Networks (CDNs) handle this by sending a separate copy of the video to each viewer via unicast—one stream for each person. This approach wastes bandwidth because the same bits travel the same network links multiple times. IP multicast could solve this by sending one copy that the network replicates where needed, but multicast has failed to gain widespread Internet adoption despite decades of effort. TreeDN is a new architecture that solves this problem by combining simplified multicast with overlay tunneling technology.
sections.eli5: When millions of people watch one live event, the Internet sends billions of copies of each frame. TreeDN sends only one copy and makes the network replicate it like branches of a tree.

sections.title: Why Multicast Failed and What TreeDN Does Differently
sections.content: IP multicast suffered from three fundamental problems. First, the "All or Nothing" problem: every router and firewall between the source and all receivers must support multicast. If even one link does not, the whole system fails. Second, the "It's Too Complex" problem: multicast routing protocols like PIM-SM require sophisticated configuration and troubleshooting. Third, the "Chicken and Egg" problem: there is no multicast content because there are no multicast-enabled viewers, and there are no viewers because there is no content. TreeDN avoids these problems by using Source-Specific Multicast (SSM), which is vastly simpler—it requires no network-based source discovery, only application-layer coordination. It combines SSM with Automatic Multicast Tunneling (AMT), which lets unicast-only networks tunnel into the multicast network. This creates an incremental deployment path: each network can adopt multicast independently, and viewers without multicast access can still participate via tunnels.
sections.eli5: Old multicast required every router to support it or nothing worked. TreeDN lets you skip the routers that do not support multicast by sending the data through a tunnel, so you can deploy it piece by piece.

sections.title: The TreeDN Architecture: Native Multicast and Overlays
sections.content: TreeDN has two components. The native on-net component uses Source-Specific Multicast on networks that support it. Receivers specify both a source address and a group address using IGMPv3 (for IPv4) or MLDv2 (for IPv6), and the last-hop router immediately joins the shortest-path tree without needing shared trees or source discovery. This simplicity eliminates most of the operational complexity of traditional multicast. The data plane can use any SSM-capable technology: PIM-SSM, mLDP, BIER, or Segment Routing. The overlay component extends reach to unicast-only networks. An AMT Gateway on a unicast-only client builds a tunnel to an AMT Relay at the border of the multicast network, and the relay forwards multicast traffic through the tunnel. This combination makes multicast incrementally deployable: operators need only support SSM natively and ensure AMT relays are available for off-net clients. Over time, the cost of carrying unicast tunnels provides incentive for more networks to enable native multicast.
sections.eli5: On networks that support multicast, use normal multicast. On networks that do not, use a tunnel to reach a nearby box that does. Either way, the viewer gets the stream.

sections.title: Replication-as-a-Service and Cost Savings
sections.content: TreeDN enables Replication-as-a-Service (RaaS): operators can offer content providers a new service where they send one stream and the network replicates it to all viewers. Unlike traditional unicast CDNs, which require content storage, key management, and per-viewer TCP connections, a TreeDN provider simply forwards multicast packets. No storage is needed. The provider uses existing infrastructure: routers that already support SSM and simple AMT relays. For operators with routers that support AMT natively, new RaaS functionality can be offered at potentially zero additional cost in equipment. The provider collects accounting data (traffic volume, number of AMT tunnels) for billing, but that is simpler than managing a full CDN. Traditional CDNs incur per-viewer costs, but TreeDN's marginal cost of adding one more viewer to a multicast stream approaches zero from the network's perspective.
sections.eli5: A service provider can offer replication as a service without buying lots of expensive CDN boxes, just by using their existing network routers and adding a few tunnel servers.

sections.title: Real-World TreeDN Deployments
sections.content: TreeDN is not theoretical. The EUMETCast Terrestrial service, operated by the European Organisation for the Exploitation of Meteorological Satellites (EUMETSAT), delivers real-time satellite data for climate monitoring and anomaly detection. It connects to the GEANT research network and uses a global deployment of AMT relays to serve both multicast-enabled and unicast-only receivers. The RARE network is a global testbed interconnecting research and education networks using routers running BIER (Bit Index Explicit Replication) as the data plane, with AMT relays deployed globally. The Multicast Menu is a web portal that lists and launches multicast streams available on a TreeDN network spanning multiple research networks. These deployments show that the architecture works in practice, handles encryption, authorization, and reliability, and can deliver critical services such as meteorological data distribution.
sections.eli5: Real services are already using TreeDN to deliver satellite data to research networks. They have tested it with different network equipment and it works.

items.title: All or Nothing
items.text: AMT overlays let unicast-only networks tunnel into multicast networks; no longer requires every hop

items.title: Too Complex
items.text: SSM with out-of-band source discovery eliminates need for complex shared-tree routing protocols

items.title: Chicken and Egg
items.text: Incremental deployment: operators enable SSM independently; tunnels let viewers join immediately
